name: Yoga for posture

lead: Postural yoga uses poses, stretches and breathing to loosen tight chest and hip areas and build awareness of how you hold yourself. People use it to slouch less and stand taller and more open.

The chain is better mobility and alignment, a weaker slouching habit, then a more upright standing look. Reviews cited on Wikipedia report moderate-quality evidence that yoga reduces back pain, and small studies report stress reduction from short sessions. A 2017 study mapped core muscle activation across yoga postures. No controlled trial of yoga changing standing posture or visible appearance was found.

paras: People practise in classes, at home or with videos, often a few sessions a week, mixing stretches, strength holds and breathing. It is commonly combined with strength training. Changes in flexibility and body awareness tend to build over weeks of regular practice.

Case reports describe glaucomatous optic nerve damage progressing in people who regularly practised the headstand, with eye pressure rising when the head is down. Inverted poses are the main flagged concern; people with glaucoma or eye-pressure conditions may want to avoid them. Overstretching can cause strains like any exercise.

angle.text: Postural yoga loosens tight chest and hip areas and builds alignment awareness, so you slouch less and stand taller and more open. Studies cover back pain and stress; its effect on visible posture has been tested very little.

lead: Yoga for posture refers to using yoga asanas (physical poses) to improve flexibility, strength and alignment. Modern postural yoga was developed in the early twentieth century, revived in the 1920s by teachers such as Yogendra and Kuvalayananda and spread by students of Tirumalai Krishnamacharya, including B.K.S. Iyengar, whose Light on Yoga (1966) helped popularise it worldwide.[1]

Evidence is strongest for back pain: reviews cited on Wikipedia, including a 2017 review, report moderate-quality evidence that yoga reduces back pain.[1] Small experimental studies show stress-reduction effects of short yoga sessions.[2] No trial found has tested yoga for changing standing posture or appearance.
infobox: Moderate for back pain; none found for posture appearance

paras: Older yoga traditions were not centred on postures. Posture-based yoga was revived in the 1920s, and Krishnamacharya in Mysore combined Hatha yoga with wrestling exercises and Western gymnastics from the 1930s to the 1950s. European physical culture also influenced it.[1] Historian William Broad argues that scientific health claims for yoga began as Hindu nationalist posturing, and Kuvalayananda reportedly found no evidence for his claims about shoulderstand and the endocrine glands.[1]

A 2012 study of 20 office workers compared 15 minutes of chair-based yoga postures and guided meditation with usual work; both reduced perceived stress compared with control.[2] A 2017 anatomical study examined core muscle activation in different yogic postures.[3] A 2023 meta-analysis examined yoga and pulmonary function in asthma.[4]

Wikipedia cites a systematic review of six studies finding Iyengar yoga effective, at least short term, for neck and low back pain, and a 2017 review finding moderate-quality evidence for reduced back pain; a 2014 report called yoga extremely understudied.[1] No studies found measuring change in postural alignment or appearance.

Case reports describe progression of glaucomatous optic neuropathy and visual field loss in patients who practised the Sirsasana (headstand) daily for years, with intraocular pressure rising significantly in the head-down position.[5][6]
